TC-017: Looks for exposed admin panels, directory listings, debug error pages, leftover install/backup files, and missing security headers (CORS, CSP, clickjacking, HSTS, cache) that give an attacker a free foothold.
TC-022: Tries common and vendor-specific default username/password pairs against login and admin interfaces that were never changed from their factory settings.
TC-025: Checks whether the application accepts short, common, or breached passwords, and whether it enforces complexity or reuse rules when a password is changed.
TC-027: Probes the password-reset flow for predictable tokens, tokens that don't expire, and resets that don't require the current password or properly invalidate old sessions.
TC-050: Confirms that pages and actions meant to require login or a specific role actually enforce that on the server, not just by hiding a button in the UI.
TC-052: Attempts to gain higher privileges by tampering with role/privilege values in a request, or by chaining a compromised low-privilege account into admin access.
TC-053: Substitutes another user's ID into a URL, query parameter, or request body to see whether their data is returned without an ownership check.
TC-054: The API version of IDOR -- checks read, update, and delete operations on individual records to confirm the server verifies the caller actually owns the object.
TC-055: Checks whether admin-only actions and hidden or undocumented endpoints are reachable by a lower-privileged or anonymous user.
TC-056: Attempts to escalate privileges by directly tampering with a role value carried in a query parameter, request body, cookie, or custom header.
TC-057: Tampers with a JWT's role claim and signature (including switching to alg:none or brute-forcing a weak signing secret) to see if a forged token is accepted.
TC-085: Checks for deserialization weaknesses via safe structural and fingerprinting probes -- deliberately never sends a real exploit payload, since that would be an actual remote-code-execution attempt against a live system.
TC-099: Attempts to upload files designed to execute code on the server (web shells, executables) to confirm upload validation actually blocks them.
TC-100: Tests file-type, size, and filename validation on upload endpoints, including double-extension tricks and path traversal via the filename.
TC-105: Scans API and page responses for personal data (emails, card numbers, SSNs), leftover backup/source files, and secrets left in error messages, comments, or browser storage.
TC-116: For GraphQL targets, checks whether queries and mutations enforce per-field and per-object authorization, and flags an open introspection endpoint separately.
TC-127: Injects crafted values into every discovered input point (parameters, JSON bodies, headers, cookies) to detect error-based, blind, and time-based SQL injection -- detection only, never real data extraction.
TC-128: Injects a unique marker into every input point to check whether it executes as script -- covers reflected, stored, and DOM-based XSS with real in-browser execution confirmation.
TC-129: Checks session handling end to end: fixation, missing logout invalidation, no login-attempt rate limiting, insecure cookie flags, predictable session tokens, and unbounded session lifetime.
TC-130: Confirms that state-changing actions actually require and validate an anti-CSRF token bound to the current session, not just a cookie.
TC-131: For multi-tenant applications, checks whether swapping the organization/workspace identifier in a request lets one tenant see another tenant's data.
TC-132: Where a security-question recovery flow exists, flags it if the question is drawn from a well-known list of easily-guessable prompts.
TC-133: Tries small variations in how a protected URL is requested (case, trailing characters, encoding tricks) to see if any bypass the authentication check entirely.
TC-134: Checks whether duplicate request parameters are handled inconsistently, and whether user-supplied text would survive unescaped into a spreadsheet export.
TC-135: Tests registration and multi-step workflows for logic gaps -- reserved username takeover, role injection at signup, and skipping directly to a later step in a flow.
TC-136: Confirms whether a manipulated request can poison a shared cache for other visitors, or trick the cache into serving a private page as if it were public.
TC-137: Attempts to make the server fetch attacker-chosen internal or external URLs -- covering cloud metadata endpoints, internal port scanning, alternate-encoding bypasses, and out-of-band confirmation.
